**Verdict:** Raise your prices first. Hormozi would say a 4-person agency at $35k/month ($420k a year) is far below the level where he calls "simply charging more" one of the biggest levers in a business. Adding clients at today's prices mostly adds work for the same four people.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. He hasn't talked about a marketing agency in particular, but he has addressed the "raise prices or get more volume" choice for a small service business in detail.

**Why he'd say it**
- **He'd first ask what's limiting you.** "the first problem I try to delineate is this is a supply constraint business or a demand constraint business." ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=227s) @ 3:47) Four people delivering client work are probably short on capacity, not on leads. More clients at the same price makes that worse. He warns owners about fixing a problem in a way that "makes your existing problem worse" (@ 4:19).
- **He thinks higher prices are often easier to sell.** "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up." ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s) @ 7:00) He also says it gets you better clients: "you increase the emotional investment, you increase the perceived value, you increase the results, and you decrease the demandingness of the customer." (@ 7:33). Demanding clients are what wear down a small agency.
- **He calls it a top lever at your size.** "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business is simply charging more because people actually believe you can deliver the service now." ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s) @ 8:06) He applies this to owners under about $3–5M in revenue.
- **He has a test for whether you're underpriced.** "whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale." Before raising, work out the close rate where the higher price earns the same as now: "As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money." (@ 8:06)
- **He'd point you at clients who value it most.** "if you're going to go Hook Fish go to go where the whales are". The same work is worth far more to a bigger client ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6018s) @ 1:40:18). He also says "when you have demand, cut supply" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=328s) @ 5:28).
- **He'd add a premium tier priced about 10x higher.** A few buyers at that price add up, and even if nobody takes it, it makes your main offer look more valuable. "You must confront the high price." ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=489s) @ 8:09)

**What he's done**
- **A PR agency (the closest case to yours).** At one of his portfolio companies, a PR agency with high churn, he found the 15% of clients who bought the top package and stayed. He rebuilt the agency around only that niche (founders raising money) and raised prices 10x, and response rates went up ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4991s) @ 1:23:11).
- **An HVAC-cleaning business.** The owner raised prices 23% and closed more deals. Hormozi then proposed another 10%, which he calculated as about 25% more net profit at the same volume ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=386s) @ 6:26).

**What would change his answer**
- **Leads are your real limit.** If you have spare capacity and not enough leads, his playbook switches to getting more customers. His first move there is to push your existing channel harder before opening a new one.
- **Your close rate is already low.** Then a raise could drop you below the break-even close rate, and he presents the raise as "more asking than telling."
- **Your ideal clients say the price is the problem.** Then he'd add a lower tier rather than raise the price. If clients you don't want complain, he says to ignore them, because the price is doing its job as a filter.

To use his test, check your close rate on proposals over the last few months. If it's above about 80%, he'd treat that as a clear sign to raise prices. Keep in mind that his free content is also a funnel into Acquisition.com, so it naturally favors bold pricing moves.

Checked the vault. I'm writing up the answer now. The best match is a 2026 consult Hormozi did with a duct-cleaning company, which is very close to your situation.

**Verdict:** Spend it on ads, but fix the ad's landing page and the creative before you raise the budget. Hire salespeople only if you already know you can close sales face to face, for example by knocking on doors. For a local service business, Hormozi puts outbound selling, which takes a lot of people, at the end of the list and the cheap marketing fixes at the start. Before either, he'd ask whether you even have the cleaners to handle more customers.

**Based on:** mostly said it, in a consult with a similar business (HVAC duct cleaning, about $1.25M a year). The rest follows from what he said.

**Why he'd say it**
- **First question: can you handle more demand?** "the first problem I try to delineate is this is a supply constraint business or a demand constraint business." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 3:47, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=227s). He warns that owners often fix a problem "that if you fix it, makes your existing problem worse" (@ 4:19). If your crews are already fully booked, neither ads nor a salesperson is the answer. Hire and keep cleaners first.
- **Cheap fixes come first, outbound comes last.** He gave the duct-cleaning owner a ranked list: raise prices 10%, build an ad landing page, fix the ads, raise ad spend, send reactivation emails to past customers, add retargeting and branded search. Outbound selling to HOAs came last (@ 30:45). His reasoning: "if we fix the landing page and we just improve the ads you have you might already double or triple your lead flow." (@ 31:48). "Like no Hail Mary's. This is just consistent yardage." (@ 4:19).
- **Once ads pay back, spend as much as they allow.** If you know the ads are bringing in the money, the answer to how much to spend "would be as many dollars as you possibly could." (@ 11:21). But "if you're not sure, then you have a data problem. So, you got to go make sure the attribution's right." So track every booking back to the ad it came from before you scale the $10k.
- **When ads stall, the creative is usually the reason**, not the platform: "the creative unlock is usually why someone gets limited." ([[yt-MH-IMJxbUY4]] @ 12:00, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=720s).

**When he'd pick the salesperson instead:** in another consult, the owner of a two-month-old roofing company could close about one sale for every 20 doors he knocked. There Hormozi said to go all in on sales: "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." and "It's what you're good at." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 9:49, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s). His rule is "focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now" (@ 3:16). He'd scale it by building a team of door-to-door reps paid commission per door, and by recruiting reps as carefully as customers: "think about sales people as your new customers or your new avatar." (@ 21:45). So if you already get cleaning clients by knocking doors or calling businesses yourself, put the $10k into commission-based reps who copy what you do.

**What he did:** the duct-cleaning owner followed the list and reported going from about $1.25M to a projected $2.3–2.5M a year later, with leads up from about 120 to about 200 a month. Those are the guest's own figures, and he also credits a new marketing agency.

**What would change his answer:**
- If you're short on cleaners, the money goes to hiring cleaners, not to either option.
- If you're already a proven face-to-face closer, it goes to salespeople.
- If you can't tell which bookings your ads produced, fix the tracking before spending more.

**Not in the vault:** $10k doesn't pay a salaried salesperson for long. His roofing example only works with commission-only pay, which also caps your downside.

Note that these consult videos double as promotion for Acquisition.com, so they show his best cases. I don't disagree with his advice here.

**Verdict:** Cut it down. Hormozi would say more workouts and content will probably make your churn worse. Find the one or two things your members actually use, make those excellent, and get new members a win in their first 24 hours.

His reasoning: people who pay for five things and use one feel they're getting 20% of what they paid for. Content they never touch just gives them a reason to cancel.

**Based on:** he said it. He addressed this case directly, and his main example is a fitness business.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Overwhelm is the main reason people cancel.** "The number one reason people churn, outside of price, is overwhelm. It is the churn driver. And this is why doing less can often retain more." ([How to Get Your Customers to Stay FOREVER](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=558s) @ 9:18, 2026). He says these numbers apply to online and consumer services, and names weight-loss services as an example.
- **Extra content lowers how much value people feel they get.** "When you have five things that you pay for, but you only use one, you feel like you're only getting 20% of the value. If for the same price, you just offer that one thing, people feel like they're getting 100% of the value." Adding things means "all we did is we gave them more reason to cancel because they never used it" ([@ 10:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=622s)).
- **The fitness example.** Planet Fitness surveyed health-club members and found most only used the cardio machines and some weights, about 10–15% of the facility. So it sold just that, for $10 a month. He also tells of a community on Skool (his community platform) that deleted content and went from 30% monthly churn to 5%, which he calls a 6x increase in lifetime value.
- **Your members have lives.** "people who are using your services are not full-time using your stuff… we want to think about value per second, not seconds of value." Online, that might mean "one post, one call recording, or just one single action" a week ([@ 11:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=686s)).
- **Simple takes more work, not less.** "complexity is typically the child of lazy thinking." His test is "how much can I take away and still have it be good… it probably is better" ([Less is More](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s) @ 11:02, 2025).

**What to do, in his steps**
1. **Ask the people who cancel why they're leaving.** Use a short DM script, tag each reason in a spreadsheet (price, overwhelm, not using it, not what they expected), and every 20 or so cancellations fix the top one or two reasons. Don't react to any single answer.
2. **Ask your longest members why they stay.** Whatever keeps coming up is what keeps people. "If you can only do one thing that gets people to stay, why would you do five?"
3. **Run the "fight for" survey.** Ask: "if I were to delete everything, what one thing would you fight for?" Also ask which one thing they wouldn't miss. Keep the top one or two and mostly drop the rest.
4. **Make two paths.** Give busy members a clear "start here" and a simple weekly routine, like 3 workouts a week. Keep the deeper material optional for keen members.
5. **Put the best thing at the start.** "pin the fast win up front so new members hit that value ideally within the first 24 hours."

**What he's done himself:** In his own Skool Games community, the top reason people cancelled was overwhelm. He cut the live calls from three a week to one, moved the big monthly download to quarterly, and turned off some app features.

**What would change his answer:** He'd only add something if your cancellation reasons pointed to a real gap, like "missing feature" or "not what I expected" coming up again and again, and even then only "when it's required or necessary for that person to get the desired value." If price comes up most often from your ideal customers, he'd suggest a lower tier or a discounted annual plan instead.

For scale, he gives Skool's average as 80% monthly retention. If fewer than 7 in 10 members stay each month, he says retention should be your top priority.

**Verdict:** Keep the 9-to-5 for now. Hormozi would tell you the job isn't what's stopping you. Use the hours around it to build the business, cut your costs, and save cash so you can afford risk later. Quitting now with no savings and no revenue isn't the kind of risk he means when he says risk gets rewarded.

**Based on:** partly things he said directly, partly what follows from them. He talks to 9-to-5 workers directly, but he never gives an exact point at which to quit.

**Why he'd say it**
- **The job isn't the problem; your spare hours are.** "Your nine-to-five job is not killing your dreams." He says the waste is in "your five to nine in the morning and your five to nine at night." ([1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=194s) @ 3:14, 3:46)
- **A job isn't the high-risk option some people claim.** "as much as the entrepreneur talking heads want to say being an employee nowadays is riskier than owning a business. That's not really true." He also concedes that "the vast majority of entrepreneurs make less." ([2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=66s) @ 1:06; [3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1546s) @ 25:46)
- **You need money in the bank before you can take risk.** "The first step is that we have to cut all costs, so that we can take more risk." And: "you get rewarded for the risk you take on. You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money." He says he felt wealthiest at $100K in the bank, because "You can't think about your long-term vision if you're trying to pay rent." ([1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=32s) @ 0:32, 13:04)
- **The pay goes to risk that looks bigger than it is.** The best bets look "very risky for other people and not risky at all for them." Quitting with a few paying customers and a year of savings fits that. Quitting with nothing doesn't. (@ 8:16 in [2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=496s). Applying this to your quit decision is my reading, not his words.)

**What he's done:** At 22 he quit a consulting job he hated and drove to California to open a gym. It took six months from deciding to actually doing it. He calls it "the hardest decision" of his life. Even after the gym was paying him about $20K a month, he kept paying about $400 a month to share a bedroom so he could save. ([4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=435s) @ 7:15)

**What would change his answer:**
- **The job feels like a cage.** In that case he says "sometimes you have to let other people's dreams for your life die for yours to live" (the transcript has "streams"). He was grateful he hated his job, because otherwise "I don't think I would have left." ([4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=3239s) @ 53:59, 1:49:04)
- **The job feels fine.** Then "maybe you just need to like the life you have and that's cool too." (@ 57:50)
- **You have nothing to lose.** He calls "a capped downside, an uncapped upside" "the recipe for opportunity" (the transcript reads "capp"). (@ 15:09 in [3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=909s))

**Things to keep in mind:**
- The vault doesn't record a specific point (an amount of revenue or months of savings) at which he says to quit. "Quit once the side business pays and you have savings to live on" is my extrapolation from the points above.
- His frugality advice assumes you have no dependents.
- His own story is a survivor's story. He went broke after the gym, and the vault notes that survivorship bias in his advice.

**Verdict:** Offer a guarantee, not a no-refunds policy. Make it a conditional one: if the client does the agreed work and doesn't get the promised result, you refund them or keep coaching them free until they do. Hormozi's view is that you get paid more by taking on the buyer's risk, and that a coaching offer is worth more the more certain the buyer feels of getting the result.

**Based on:** follows from what he said, plus *$100M Offers*, which is not in the vault. The vault doesn't cover refund policies for coaching directly.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Taking on risk is something you sell.** "you can absolutely sell a guarantee. You can absolutely sell a warranty." He says this works in any business: "you can always inject these things into a business, no matter what type of business you have." ([6 Levels of Making Money @ 13:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=790s)) His general rule is that pay tracks the risk you carry. A no-refunds policy pushes all the risk onto the client, which puts you lower on his pyramid.
- **Certainty is one of the four parts of his value equation.** The ideal offer is one where "they'd be virtually guaranteed they would get it it would happen immediately and it would be effortless" ([Diary of a CEO @ 1:22:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4928s)). At $2,000, the buyer's real question is "will this work for me?" A guarantee answers it.
- **He refunds when he misses the promise.** His speed-fee example: "if you want us to get this done um for sure by the end of the week and if we don't we don't even charge it." ([Scale or Fail @ 18:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1113s))
- **The exception: a strong reputation can replace an explicit guarantee.** "your reputation over time acts as almost an implied guarantee", as long as buyers believe you're competent and want to help them ([If I Started A Business in 2026 @ 14:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=885s)). He also says one-on-one delivery makes buyers feel much more likely to succeed (@ 14:12). If you already have lots of case studies and referrals, you need the explicit guarantee less. If you're early, you need it more.

**How he'd set it up** *(from $100M Offers, not in the vault)*: For services, he prefers conditional guarantees tied to what the client has to do, like attending every call or finishing the assignments. That stops refunds from people who didn't do the work, and it gets clients to engage, which helps them get results. He also describes an "all sales final" anti-guarantee, but only when you give a real reason for it, such as revealing proprietary material up front. A strict no-refunds policy with no reason is the weakest choice in his framework.

**What would change his answer:** If you have so much demand that you're turning people away, you can rely on your reputation as the implied guarantee and spend your effort raising the price instead. That follows from his supply-constrained pricing advice; he hasn't said it about guarantees directly.

**Verdict:** Pay off the car loan and the credit cards first. Then put what's left into the business, but only into things that have already shown they pay back. Hormozi leans toward Dave Ramsey on debt: he thinks debt adds risk that eventually comes due, and he wants your car "paid off so you don't have to think about it again."

**Based on:** he talked about the car directly, and the rest follows from what he's said. The vault has nothing on consumer credit cards specifically.

**Why he'd say it**
- **On the car, he said it outright.** In his video on banking your first $100K, he puts the car under cutting costs: "ideally a paid-off clunker is the best way to go… ideally just pay off your car so you don't have to think about it again." ([video @ 2:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=128s))
- **He's against debt in general.** "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side and the single argument that I have around it is basically debt increases risk. Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." He adds that "businesses have seasons, they have volatility", and that companies that last, like Chick-fil-A, "operate debt free." ([video @ 8:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s))
- **He admits part of it is peace of mind**, not just math: "I'd say this is more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing." (same video @ 8:37) Elsewhere he says that having $100K in the bank was "when I stopped having to worry about tomorrow," and that "You can't think about your long-term vision if you're trying to pay rent." ([video @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk))
- **You cut costs so you can take risks, not instead of taking them.** "The first step is that we have to cut all costs, so that we can take more risk." Later: "you get rewarded for the risk you take on. You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money." (same video @ 0:32 and [@ 13:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=784s)) Clearing monthly payments frees up cash every month that you can put back into the business.
- **When the money does go into the business, he wants it to go where returns are proven.** He'd spend heavily on ads that already return several dollars per dollar. But "if you're not sure, then you have a data problem. So, you got to go make sure the attribution's right." ([video @ 11:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=681s)) He doesn't back putting everything into an untested idea.

**What he's done:** He coached an HVAC owner who had $60k of business debt and planned to clear it in 4–5 months. Hormozi said "Okay, good," and put "continue to pay off the debt" second on the owner's priority list. That was even though the owner's ads were returning 13:1 and Hormozi wanted ad spend raised as well ([video @ 30:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s)). In other words, a business with great returns still didn't make carrying debt acceptable to him. He also lived on $400 a month in rent while his gym paid him about $20k a month, and saved the difference to spend on growth.

**What would change his answer:** He'd lean harder toward the business if you already have a channel with clear numbers, for example proven ad returns at scale. "If for every dollar you gave me, I gave you $5 back," your budget should be "as many dollars as you possibly could." (@ 11:21) Even then, his own coaching example paid down the debt and grew at the same time.

**Not in the vault:** Credit cards. Typical 20%+ card interest is a guaranteed loss that almost no reinvestment reliably beats. That's just how his Ramsey-leaning logic applies here, not something the vault quotes him saying. He'd pay those off before the car.

**My own view, beyond his:** Keep a few months of expenses in cash rather than spending all $50k. The vault doesn't show him addressing a cash reserve, though his "$100K in the bank" idea points the same way.

**Verdict:** Do both, but not as two separate projects. Make short-form clips the thing you post often and test hard, and treat long-form as the source you cut them from. If you can only keep up one, pick short-form, post a lot of it, and turn the clips that win into ads.

**Based on:** mostly follows from what he said. The vault has no clip where he directly compares long-form and short-form for audience growth. His content advice in the vault is all short-form, and his general rules (volume, one channel, test and scale winners) decide the rest.

**Why he'd say it**
- **When a business owner wants more reach, he tells them to do more short-form.** In a 2026 consult, the guest said shorts were "very painful and slow growth." His answer was to find a native editor ("one hyper-caffeinated uh 20-year-old who lives and is brain-rotted Gen Z", [yt-MH-IMJxbUY4 @ 11:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=688s)) and to fix the hooks, use trending audio and drop the polish. It shouldn't look professional; iPhone-selfie style is fine.
- **Short-form pays twice.** "when you find your winners, just take that same post, add a 5-second CTA at the end, and then run that as an ad." He also says "It's a double dip because you're posting content and they don't have to waste any money" ([@ 13:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=820s)). Organic posts are a free way to test ads.
- **Copy what already works in your niche.** "I would look at the top travel pages, look at the most viral content they have, and model that" ([@ 15:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=950s)).
- **Volume decides it.** "you just have to do so much volume that it is unreasonable that you fail" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 9:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=544s)). Short-form gets you the most attempts and the fastest feedback.
- **One channel until it works.** "you want to sell one product or service to one avatar on one channel until you make $1 million." ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 8:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=489s)). So he wouldn't have you running a podcast, a YouTube channel and three short-form accounts at once.
- **Give away real value.** His content is free and goes "wide and deep" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 3:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=236s)), with the aim "to hopefully provide more value to a company before they've ever spoken to us" ([@ 2:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=172s)). Long-form is where that depth lives, and it's what turns someone who watched a clip into a buyer.

**What he's done (not in the vault):** His own channel works like this. He records long talks and podcasts, and his team cuts them into many short clips across platforms. In his view, short-form brings people in and long-form earns their trust. This is from what I know of him, not from a quote in this vault.

**What would change his answer:** He says short-form is easy in visual niches like travel, and that for something like a tax-savings business "it's tougher" and you'd need an emotional, story-based angle ([@ 7:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=458s)). If your product doesn't show well on camera, lean more on long-form explanation and stories. He also puts offers first: content can't save a weak offer.

The vault is thin on this exact question. It has one consult that touches it and no dedicated talk on content strategy. Adding his videos on content and audience growth would firm this up if you want me to add sources.

**Verdict:** Keep full price. Hormozi wouldn't take 30% off. He'd use Black Friday as a real, time-limited reason to buy and make the offer better instead: add bonuses, add a premium tier, or add an annual or bundle option, and set a deadline you actually keep.

His reasoning is that price signals whether you can deliver. A 30% cut lowers that signal and cuts your margin. It also teaches your audience to wait for the next sale.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing from him on Black Friday or percentage discounts specifically.

**Why he'd say it**
- **A higher price raises perceived value.** "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up" ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s)). And: "if you raise your price, you increase the emotional investment, you increase the perceived value, you increase the results, and you decrease the demandingness of the customer" (@ 7:33). A discount does the reverse: buyers trust the result less and commit less.
- **Most owners undercharge.** "they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" (@ 7:33). For businesses under about $3–5M in revenue he calls charging more "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business" (@ 8:06).
- **If not enough people buy, fix the offer, not the price.** "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:25:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5123s)). The levers are his value equation: dream outcome, likelihood of success, speed and ease. Price isn't one of them.
- **Urgency only works if it's real.** "the key to making urgency and scarcity work is making it legitimate" ([yt-JDR-R--4HhM @ 21:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1310s)). When the deadline passes, "you say no and you say no so you can maintain the reputation" (@ 22:29). A sale people know will come back costs you that reputation: "everyone knows it doesn't matter because you're not going to sell out and that's where you start losing power" (@ 23:05). So keep the Black Friday deadline, but put a bonus or a limited number of spots behind it, not a price cut.
- **Earn more per buyer instead.** "do what you can control, make more from each one" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)). He'd put a premium tier at about 10x the price next to the course, such as the course plus one-on-one time: "You lift your entire brand because if you charge $10,000 an hour, something absurd, it doesn't matter" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 7:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=425s)).

- Add a premium tier.

**Verdict:** He probably wouldn't promote your best rep just because they sell the most. He'd give the job to someone who can track numbers and train reps. **Based on:** mostly beyond the vault. The vault's 10 sources never compare an outside hire with promoting a top rep. Nothing he said there settles it, but a few nearby principles point the same way.

**Why he'd say it**
- **The job is tracking, not selling.** He told a roofing owner who was adding salespeople that as the team grows, "you're going to probably have to track this maybe a little bit more than you are right now" and "this is going to probably be the next piece that you're going to want to have to install." ([yt-o64cI6tebnU @ 21:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1274s), [@ 21:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1305s)) Choose the person who can build and run that tracking. Being good at closing doesn't show they can.
- **At about 4–5 reps, the owner may not need a manager yet.** That owner had four or five people, and the vault's notes say Hormozi told him he could probably manage that many reps himself. The quote for this isn't in the vault, so treat it as a paraphrase. Hiring a manager too early adds a layer before you have a real constraint to fix.
- **Your best rep is your training material.** His advice to new salespeople is to shadow the best rep and do twice their volume ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo)). If you move your best rep off the phones, you lose your top producer and the example the others learn from.
- **He's against fear-based managers.** "if people are afraid of me then they will immediately comply and it's effective for short durations but not for long durations" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 16:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=971s)). Whoever runs the team needs to lead people, not just hit a number.
- **Beyond the vault:** in his other content, as far as I recall, he warns that promoting your top seller often costs you a great rep and gets you a mediocre manager. He also tends to say "hire people who've already done the thing" for roles you can't do yourself. I'm fairly but not fully confident of this, and the vault doesn't back it.

**What would change his answer:** If your best rep already coaches others, looks at their numbers, and wants the job, promoting from within fits his focus on culture. If they want to be the manager only for the title or the money, a commission plan that keeps them selling fits his thinking better.

**My caveat:** I think "best rep vs. outsider" is less important than testing whoever you pick: have them run your pipeline tracking and coach two reps for 30 days before you give them the title.

**Verdict:** Double down on the first business. Hormozi's documented view is that a second line splits the resources your one working bet needs, and that at $1M the growth you're looking for is probably still inside the first business.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. He talks about focus and saying no to new opportunities, but nothing in the vault answers "$1M business, second line or not?" directly.

**Why he'd say it**

- **A second business is a "second bridge."** His strategy question is "what one thing if it were true 12 months from now would change everything for our business," and he warns: "Sometimes you have to sit with the pain of an unbuilt bridge without building a second bridge." Doing it two or three ways "ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work but will take time." ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 4:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=298s), @ 6:04)
- **The pull toward a second line comes from success, and that's the warning sign.** "the more capable you get, the more resources you have at your disposal, the more opportunities present themselves, the more the harder it is to consistently say no" (yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 8:17). In 2025: "the effort that it takes to compound is the length of time you have to say no to everything else" and "The price of wanting to be good at everything is being good at nothing." ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 22:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1378s), @ 22:24)
- **You probably need a better money model, not a different business.** "A lot of business owners think that they need to change something about their business or get into a different business." His answer is "your actual money model… How you collect money, how you charge for what you do." When getting customers is hard or expensive: "do what you can control, make more from each one." ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 3:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=201s), @ 3:55, @ 8:50) In practice that means price increases, upsells, a premium tier and recurring memberships.
- **Grow means more customers or worth more, and you work the existing channel first.** He first finds out whether a business is limited by supply or by demand. Then he leans toward pushing the current channel harder: "there's a lot more that you can work on the existing one by like a lot," and "New channel, little too hard for right now." ([yt-MH-IMJxbUY4 @ 5:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=327s), @ 24:06) If a new channel is too much of a stretch, a whole new business is a bigger one.
- **He's done this at your size.** In 2026 he consulted for a duct-cleaning business doing about $1.25M a year. Every lever he pulled was inside that one business: higher prices, a landing page, ad creative, reactivation emails and an affiliate offer. A year later the owner was projecting $2.3–2.5M ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4)).

**What he's done:** He did start second businesses: Prestige Labs (supplements) and ALAN (software), both funded from profits. But he launched Prestige Labs once Gym Launch was already big. By his account Gym Launch made $26M in its first full year, and Prestige Labs was sold to "thousands of gym owners that had licensed" his model ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo)). So the second business sold to his existing customers. It wasn't a new market started at $1M. He also admits he gets impatient after about 30 days and starts a second approach, and calls that a mistake he's trying to stop.

**What would change his answer:** He never states a size where a second line makes sense; the following is my reading of his own history. He'd likely say yes when the first business has stopped being where your growth is coming from, when the new line sells to customers you already have, and when it makes each customer worth more. Even then, he'd probably build it as an upsell inside the first business rather than as a separate company.

**Caveat:** Much of the "money model" argument comes from a video promoting his book *Money Models*, so he has a commercial interest in that answer.

**Verdict: Keep it.** By Hormozi's logic, 3x profit means you hand over the business for about three years of its own earnings. He'd want you to keep growing it, and he'd only consider selling if you need the cash to get out of a hole or want to put it into something you're sure is bigger. **Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing where he talks about a 3x offer specifically, so this applies his principles and his own exits to your situation.

**Why he'd say it**
- **The point of bootstrapping is that you choose when to sell.** He says you keep control and equity, and "you can exit on your own time horizon or never exit at all" ([sL16tsGafcQ @ 3:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=225s)). He wants you to build something that keeps paying out: "design a compounding vehicle... and then you let that over time do the heavy lifting" (@ 4:19). Selling at 3x means someone else gets the compounding.
- **His own sale was partial.** In 2021 he and Leila sold two-thirds of Gym Launch and Prestige Labs at a $46.2M valuation, after already taking $42M out in distributions ([x3e73Qn6NOo @ 32:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1938s); [tGhe3sBuk34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34)). They kept a third. He also says he could have kept going: "maybe I could have stayed there and could have just continued to compound it" ([x3e73Qn6NOo @ 33:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2003s)).
- **His reason for selling was not the price.** It was what he wanted to do next: "I didn't want to be the gym guy for the rest of my life" (@ 33:23). If you don't have a clear next thing, by his reasoning you have no reason to sell.
- **His first exit went badly.** He sold his gyms because the turnaround business "makes even more money" ([x3e73Qn6NOo @ 18:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1081s)). Then "after I had all my gyms I sold them put all the money in this thing and then they all got taken" (@ 19:39). He was down to $1,000. Cashing out a business that works only to bet the money on something unproven is the mistake he made himself.
- **Pick one path and stay on it.** He says "the richest people that I know pick one of these four paths, play it for a decade" ([sL16tsGafcQ @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=0s)). Taking a quick payout cuts that decade short.

**What would change his answer**
- **You're in a financial hole.** He says to "get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible... get your oxygen mask on" ([XGm2ERU9qtA @ 17:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s)). He also says he felt wealthiest the first time he had $100K in the bank, not after his exits ([jfW6gL6hKhk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk)). If the sale ends a money crisis, taking it fits his advice.
- **You're done with the business**, the way he was done being "the gym guy." Even then, his own example was to sell a majority and keep a stake.

**Not in the vault (my read of him):** He often says a low multiple is the market's way of telling you the business depends on you as the owner. He'd probably say the better move is to remove yourself from the day-to-day, add recurring revenue and grow profit. That raises both your earnings and the multiple a buyer will pay later. A buyer offering 3x is betting they can do exactly that with your business.

**My one line of disagreement:** Three years of profit, paid in cash now and with no risk, can be a good deal if the business is shrinking, in decline, or wearing you out. Check that honestly before turning it down.

**Verdict: Hire, but only after two checks Hormozi would make first.** First, is the app actually what's holding your business back? Second, can you buy an existing tool instead of building one? If you still need it built after both, pay someone good to build it. Don't spend your own hours learning a second trade, unless software is the thing you sell.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. His "buy the tool instead of rebuilding it" point is close to something he said outright. The vault has nothing from him about AI coding tools specifically.

**Why he'd say it**

- **Is the app your constraint?** When he consults on a business, his first question is "is this a supply constraint business or a demand constraint business" ([OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 3:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=227s)). He warns that owners often "fix a problem that's already a problem that if you fix it, makes your existing problem worse" (@ 4:19). If the app doesn't bring in more customers or make each one worth more, he'd tell you not to build it.
- **Buy before you build.** On spending money early: "buy a software tool, right? That might mean like a CRM or a landing page thing… the alternative is you could try rebuild the entire thing. Yeah, or you could just like go to grab a tool that's already there. Save yourself some time." ([jfW6gL6hKhk @ 11:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=717s))
- **Pay for skill rather than grinding it out.** "The fastest way to learn skills is to find somebody who's really good and hire them one-on-one." (jfW6gL6hKhk @ 9:48) He says he did this early on, when he could barely afford it.
- **Your hours have a price.** "everyone has an hourly rate" ([uWdIgftpvBI @ 3:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=197s)). If your hour is worth more spent selling and delivering, spending months on coding is the expensive choice.
- **Promotion comes first.** He splits his day into promote, deliver and build, and puts promotion first: "if nobody knows about your stuff, they can't give you money." (jfW6gL6hKhk @ 4:49) Learning to code would take your best working hours away from that.
- **Focus.** "Sometimes you have to sit with the pain of an unbuilt bridge without building a second bridge." ([-JLN1d1ZKUU @ 4:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=298s)) Learning software development while running a business is a second bridge.

**About "10,000 iterations":** he does say skills come from volume. That advice is about the skill you sell, though. He tells people to sell "one product or service to one avatar on one channel until you make $1 million" (jfW6gL6hKhk @ 8:09). If your business is a gym or an agency, coding isn't that skill.

**What he's done:** He bootstrapped a software company, ALAN, out of his gym businesses. The vault doesn't say who wrote its code.

**What would change his answer:** If the app is the product you sell, building software becomes your core skill. Then his advice on learning through volume applies, ideally with one-on-one help from someone very good.

**Caveats:**
- The video with the tools and tutoring advice also promotes Skool, which he's involved with.
- AI coding tools come up nowhere in the vault. His AI comments are about ad creative and AI avatars, so I can't tell you whether he thinks they change the build-vs-hire math.

My own view, outside the vault: AI tools now make it cheap for a non-coder to build a rough prototype in a weekend and test whether the idea works before paying a developer. That fits his "trial attempts" spending bucket, and it doesn't commit you to learning to code.
